title.narrative: Operationalizing and implementing circular economy solutions to minimize plastic waste and reduce plastic pollution from food and beverage packaging (Plastic IP)

description.narrative: By supporting the operationalisation of circular plastic solutions, the project aims to reduce the amount of plastic waste generated by the F&B sector in India, as well as the associated emissions of Greenhouse Gases (GHG) and Persistent Organic Pollutants (POP), contributing to the GEF Focal Area 9: Chemicals of global concern and their waste reduced. The project will adopt a gender-responsive approach throughout its implementation, recognizing and addressing the differentiated roles, challenges, and opportunities for women and men in the plastic waste economy. It will actively work to collect and analyze gender-disaggregated data to better understand and highlight the significant contributions of women in tackling plastic pollution. By doing so, the project aims to adequately recognize and support women's roles in waste management, ensure equitable access to opportunities in circular economy initiatives, and address gender-specific impacts of plastic pollution. This approach will not only enhance the effectiveness of plastic reduction strategies but also promote gender equality and women's empowerment within the sector. Additionally, the project will strive to create gender-responsive economic opportunities in the circular plastics economy, particularly for women entrepreneurs and workers in the informal sector. It will also ensure that capacity-building initiatives and technology transfers are designed to be equally accessible and beneficial to both women and men, thereby promoting inclusive socio-economic development alongside environmental benefits. More specifically, each Component and Outcome will contribute to the achievement of the GEBs Core indicators as follows: Components Outcomes Contribution to the Plastic IP Components Contribution to the GEB Core Indicators Component 1: Strengthen knowledge & policy effectiveness (UNEP) Outcome 1.1: Policy coherence, effectiveness and status of implementation for sustainable plastic packaging and transition towards a circular plastics economy in the F&B sector. IP C 1: Enabling regulatory and policy environment § CI 11 - People benefiting from GEF-financed investments disaggregated by sex: 30 members of TWG (policy) and Component 2: Pilot demonstrations of redesign models to reduce problematic plastic packaging in the F&B sector (UNIDO) Outcome 2.1 Environmentally redesigned functional, and efficient plastic packaging models pilot-tested and ready for replication at the F&B sector IP C 3: Engaging with Food and Beverage Private sector § CI 9.8 – Avoided Residual Plastic Waste: Given the size and relative contribution of the 7 selected MSMEs clusters to the annual plastic waste emission in India, the piloting of sustainable packaging (re)design models to reduce plastic use might lead to about 6,500 metric tons of avoided residual plastic waste across the project lifetime. § CI 11 - People benefiting from GEF-financed investments disaggregated by sex: At least 280 people, of which at least 70 people are women (20 members of the industry TWG. There will be workshops at each cluster expecting at least 30 participants in each workshop. At least 50 participants to the outreach event). Component 3: Pilot demonstrations of Extended Producers Responsibility (EPR) schemes promoting reuse/refill-return systems for the F&B sector (UNEP) Outcome 3.1 Reduced plastic packaging consumption and waste production through EPR pilots supporting reuse/refill-return solutions in the F&B sector in two pilot cities IP C 2 : Mobilizing finance IP C 3: Engaging with Food and Beverage Private sector § CI 9.8 - Avoided Residual Plastic Waste: It has been estimated that the piloting of EPR-schemes for packaging in the cities of Pune and Shimla might lead to approximately 6,500 metric tons of avoided residual plastic waste across the project lifetime. § CI 11 - People benefiting from GEF-financed investments disaggregated by sex: Taking the average ward population of Pune (21,700) and Shimla (6,800), and assuming that the pilots will be carried out over 2-3 wards, the direct beneficiaries from Component 3 would be 85,500 direct beneficiaries (52% male and 48% female). Component 4: Capacity building and behaviour change (UNEP) Outcome 4.1 Enhanced consumer behaviour, awareness at national level, and enhanced capacities at city and state level. IP C 4: Activating Behaviour and social change to support Program strategy § CI 9.8 - Avoided Residual Plastic Waste: By helping ‘nudge’ more sustainable behaviours across the F&B plastic packaging value chain, the planned behaviour and social change interventions are also expected to contribute to about 6,500 metric tons of avoided residual plastic waste across the project lifetime. § CI 11 - People benefiting from GEF-financed investments disaggregated by sex: Direct beneficiaries from city level trainings are captured in Component 3. State level beneficiaries from trainings (Output 4.1.2) can be estimated as 100 people. Direct beneficiaries from Output 4.1.3 can be estimated as 10,000 from national campaign (budget spend USD 100/person) and 2,000 (budget spend USD 25/person) from city level behaviour change interventions. Total direct beneficiaries of Component 4 are 12,100 (52% male and 48% female). Component 5: National and Program-level Coordination, Knowledge Management and Communication (UNEP & UNIDO) Outcome 5.1. Effective National and Global Coordination including active participation and contribution to Global Project meetings and working groups Outcome 5.2 Increased National and Global knowledge and awareness on Circular Solutions to Single Use Plastic Packaging Pollution from the Food and Beverage Sector IP C 4: Activating Behaviour and social change to support Program strategy § CI 11 - People benefiting from GEF-financed investments disaggregated by sex: : Male: 51,787 and Female: 47,224 The estimated total reduction in residual plastic waste of about 19,995 metric tons will result in a reduction of 2.24 gTEQ of Persistent Organic Pollutants and of 84,469 metric tons of Greenhouse Gas emitted across the project lifetime. Addressing the consumption and production of plastics in the F&B sectors, which generate a major contribution to plastic pollution, will lead to global environmental benefits, including:§ Ecosystems and habitats preservation: Plastic pollution, including microplastics, can disrupt ecosystems, affecting everything from plankton to predators. Plastic waste can accumulate in natural habitats, altering them and making them inhospitable for many species. Minimizing plastic waste helps maintain the balance of ecosystems.§ Preservation of biodiversity: Plastic pollution can harm all types of biodiversity by disrupting food chains and habitats, provoking harm (e.g. suffocation) or potentially affecting organisms due to chemical additives in plastic. In addition, reducing plastic production and consumption can lead to lower levels of harmful chemicals released into the environment. This helps protect soil, water, and air quality, reducing the risk of contamination for both wildlife and humans.§ Reduced greenhouse gas emissions: Plastic production and incineration contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. By reducing plastic usage and properly managing plastic waste, emissions will be reduced and hence contributing to climate change mitigation.§ Landfill space conservation: Plastic waste occupies valuable landfill space, and many plastics take hundreds of years to decompose. Reducing plastic usage lessens the burden on landfills.§ Less resource depletion: Plastic production requires significant amounts of fossil fuels and natural resources. Cutting down on plastic usage conserves these resources for future generations.§ Preservation of scenic beauty: Plastic pollution detracts from the beauty of natural landscapes, coastlines, and urban areas. § Reduced chemical exposure: Approximately 4,200 out of more than 16,000 chemicals associated with plastics have been identified as substances of concern as they tend to persist without degrading, build up in the human body or other organisms, move through the environment, and for their toxicity.[1] These unreacted monomers, oligomers, and additives can leach over time, particularly during the use/consumption and End-of-Life phases. Moreover, plastic debris can absorb organic and inorganic chemicals from surrounding environment, for example, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and metals. Thus, plastic prevention helps reduce the amount of chemical contaminants entering or re-entering the environment. There are also several remarkable socio-economic benefits related to the fight against plastic pollution, as well as to promoting packaging circularity in the F&B sector. Among others, the project will contribute to:§ Cost savings: Governments spend significant resources on waste management, cleaning up plastic pollution and dealing with its consequences, such as damage to infrastructure and biodiversity. By preventing pollution at its source, these costs can be minimized, allowing funds to be allocated elsewhere.§ Job creation: Initiatives aimed at reducing plastic pollution, such as reuse systems and the development of alternative materials, create employment opportunities in various sectors, including waste/reuse management, research and development, and manufacturing. The project intends to work with local businesses in the F&B sectors to develop and pilot-test local solutions to reduce the production and consumption of plastics. These solutions, such as reuse/refill systems, tend to create orders of magnitude more jobs than disposal-based systems. Zero waste measures can be considered as an opportune social infrastructure in which investments can strengthen local economic resilience. Multiple studies of zero waste systems cite higher wages and better working conditions than in comparable fields, and opportunities to develop and use varied skills, from equipment repair to public outreach.[2]§ Innovation and entrepreneurship: Addressing plastic pollution fosters innovation in sustainable materials, F&B processing and distribution, and waste management technologies. This stimulates economic growth by creating new markets for responsible products and services. This is the case when promoting reuse and refill systems.§ Enhanced reputation: Businesses and regions that actively combat plastic pollution often enjoy improved reputations, attracting environmentally conscious consumers and investors. This can lead to increased market share, higher revenues, and greater investment inflows.§ Tourism promotion: Cleaner environments resulting from reduced plastic pollution can attract more tourists, boosting local economies reliant on tourism. Beaches, parks, and natural attractions are more appealing when free from litter and plastic debris.§ Public health improvement: Decreased plastic pollution means less plastic waste in waterways and food chains, reducing the risk of ingestion by humans and animals. This helps mitigate health issues associated with plastic contamination, such as endocrine disruption and chemical toxicity. § Community empowerment: Engaging communities, in plastic pollution reduction initiatives promotes a sense of ownership and responsibility for the environment. In addition, the project’s gender strategy will ensure gender mainstreaming and gender-specific activities in the project, such as training and business support. § Resource conservation: Minimizing plastic usage encourages the efficient use of resources, including fossil fuels used in plastic production. This supports sustainability efforts and reduces reliance on finite resources, contributing to long-term economic stability. [1] Bourzac, K. (2024, March 14).
